# Cerebrovascular system

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Basics of neurology > Cerebrovascular system*

[Original Article Link](/library/Yp0nLS)

---

## Summary

The cerebrovascular system comprises the vessels that transport blood to and from the <u>brain</u>. The <u>brain</u>'s arterial supply is provided by a pair of <u>internal carotid arteries</u> and a pair of <u>vertebral arteries</u>, the latter of which unite to form the <u>basilar artery</u>. The <u>anterior cerebral artery</u>, a branch of the <u>internal carotid artery</u>, <u>perfuses</u> the anteromedial <u>cerebral cortex</u>; the <u>middle cerebral artery</u>, a branch of the <u>internal carotid artery</u>, <u>perfuses</u> the <u>lateral</u> <u>cerebral cortex</u>; and the <u>posterior cerebral artery</u>, a branch of the <u>basilar artery</u>, <u>perfuses</u> the <u>medial</u> and <u>lateral</u> portions of the <u>posterior</u> <u>cerebral cortex</u>. The <u>internal carotid arteries</u>, the <u>anterior cerebral arteries</u>, and the <u>posterior cerebral arteries</u> <u>anastomose</u> through the <u>anterior</u> and <u>posterior communicating arteries</u> to form the <u>circle of Willis</u>, a vascular circuit surrounding the <u>optic chiasm</u> and <u>pituitary stalk</u>. The <u>circle of Willis</u> equalizes the blood flow between the cerebral hemispheres and provides anastomotic circulation, connecting the <u>anterior</u> and <u>posterior</u> cerebral circulations and, thereby, permitting continued <u>perfusion</u> of the <u>brain</u> in the event of carotid occlusion. The cerebral hemispheres are drained by <u>superficial</u> cerebral <u>veins</u> (superior cerebral <u>veins</u>, middle cerebral <u>veins</u>, inferior cerebral <u>veins</u>) and deep cerebral <u>veins</u> (<u>great cerebral vein</u>, <u>basal vein</u>), which drain into the <u>dural venous sinuses</u>. <u>Brain</u> <u>perfusion</u> is regulated by the <u>partial pressure of carbon dioxide</u> (<u>PaCO<sub>2</sub></u>). The interruption of <u>perfusion</u> due to occlusion or hemorrhage of the cerebral vessels results in a <u>stroke</u>, which manifests with <u>focal neurologic deficits</u> in the body parts controlled by the affected <u>brain</u> territory.

---

## Arterial supply

The arterial supply of the <u>brain</u> is provided by the <u>internal carotid arteries</u> and the <u>vertebral arteries</u>, which derive from branches of the <u>aortic arch</u>.




### <u>Internal carotid arteries</u> (ICA)




* Description: terminal branches of the <u>common carotid artery</u>

* Course

* Neck: lie within the <u>carotid sheath</u> and enter the <u>cranium</u> through the <u>carotid canal</u>

* <u>Cranium</u>: lie on the roof of the <u>cavernous sinus</u>, in close proximity to <u>CN VI</u>

* Branches: only have intracranial branches

* Caroticotympanic artery (the first intracranial branch of the <u>internal carotid arteries</u> that enters the <u>middle ear</u> cavity and <u>anastomoses</u> with the inferior tympanic <u>artery</u>)

* Artery of the pterygoid canal (<u>Vidian artery</u>)

* Meningohypophyseal trunk (<u>posterior</u> trunk)

* Inferolateral trunk

* <u>Ophthalmic artery</u>

* Superior <u>pituitary</u> <u>artery</u>

* <u>Posterior communicating artery</u>: <u>anastomosis</u> in <u>Circle of Willis</u>

* <u>Anterior choroidal artery</u>

* Terminal branches

* <u>Middle cerebral artery</u>: supplies <u>lateral</u> <u>cerebrum</u>

* <u>Anterior cerebral artery</u>: supplies <u>anterior</u> <u>cerebrum</u>

### Vertebral arteries




* Description: arise from the <u>subclavian arteries</u>

* Course

* Neck: The <u>vertebral arteries</u> pass through the foramina in the <u>transverse processes</u> of the <u>cervical vertebrae</u> of C1–C6 (C7 <u>transverse foramina</u> transmit only <u>veins</u>) and enter the <u>cranium</u> through the <u>foramen magnum</u>.

* <u>Cranium</u>: The right and left <u>vertebral arteries</u> unite at the midline of the <u>anterior</u> surface of the <u>pons</u> to form the <u>basilar artery</u>.

* Branches

* <u>Anterior spinal artery</u> and <u>posterior spinal arteries</u>: supply spinal cord

* <u>Posterior inferior cerebellar arteries</u> (PICA): terminal branches that supply inferior <u>cerebellum</u>

### Basilar artery




* Description: formed by the union of the two <u>vertebral arteries</u>

* Course: runs cranially in the central <u>pontine</u> groove

* Branches

* Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (<u>AICA</u>): supplies anteroinferior <u>cerebellum</u>, <u>middle cerebellar peduncle</u>, and inferolateral <u>pons</u>
* Labyrinthine artery:  supplies the <u>inner ear</u>

* Pontine arteries: supply the <u>pons</u>

* Superior cerebellar artery (<u>SCA</u>): supplies the superior surface of the <u>cerebellum</u>, superior and <u>middle cerebellar peduncles</u>, and lower <u>midbrain</u>

* <u>Posterior cerebral artery</u>: supplies occipital cortex, inferior and <u>medial</u> temporal cortices, <u>thalamus</u>, and <u>rostral</u> <u>midbrain</u>

## Circle of Willis

* Definition: a vascular circuit formed by the <u>anastomoses</u> between branches of the <u>internal carotid arteries</u> (<u>anterior</u> circulation) and <u>vertebral arteries</u> (<u>posterior</u> circulation) around the <u>optic chiasm</u> and <u>pituitary stalk</u>

* Consists of paired:

* <u>Internal carotid arteries</u> (<u>proximal</u> to the origin of the <u>middle cerebral arteries</u>)

* <u>Anterior cerebral arteries</u> (terminal branches of the internal carotids)

* <u>Posterior cerebral arteries</u> (terminal branches of the <u>vertebral arteries</u>)

* Two <u>anastomoses</u>

* Anterior communicating artery: connects the two <u>anterior cerebral arteries</u>

* Posterior communicating artery (branch of <u>internal carotid artery</u>): connects the ICA to the <u>posterior cerebral artery</u>

* Functional significance

* Equalizes arterial flow between the cerebral hemispheres

* Provides anastomotic circulation, connecting the <u>anterior</u> and <u>posterior</u> cerebral circulations and, thus, permitting continued <u>perfusion</u> of the <u>brain</u> in the event of carotid occlusion.

* Clinical significance

* <u>Berry aneurysms</u>

* <u>Saccular cerebral aneurysms</u> that most commonly occur in the <u>anterior</u> circulation of the <u>brain</u>, usually at the junction of the <u>anterior cerebral artery</u> and the <u>anterior communicating artery</u> in the <u>circle of Willis</u>.

* Most common cause of nontraumatic <u>subarachnoid hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Subclavian steal syndrome</u>

* <u>Moyamoya disease</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Most <u>saccular cerebral aneurysms</u>, also known as <u>berry aneurysms</u>, occur in the <u>anterior</u> circulation of the <u>brain</u>, usually at the junction of the <u>anterior cerebral artery</u> and the <u>anterior communicating artery</u> in the <u>circle of Willis</u>. They are the most common cause of nontraumatic <u>subarachnoid hemorrhage</u>.

## Cerebral arterial territories

| <br>Overview of cerebral arterial territories [[1]](/library/84YOO6) |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Artery</u> | Arterial territory | Main branches | Features of <u>ischemia</u>/hemorrhage |
| <u>Anterior</u> circulation (branches of the <u>internal carotid artery</u>) |  |  |  |
| <br>Anterior cerebral artery  (<u>ACA</u>) | <br>* Anteromedial cortex, including:<br><br>* <u>Medial</u> portion of the frontal and <u>parietal lobes</u>: motor and sensory supply of the lower extremities<br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> limb of the <u>internal capsule</u><br><br>* Corpus callosum<br><br>* <u>Basal ganglia</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Anterior communicating artery</u><br><br>* <u>Ophthalmic artery</u><br><br>* <u>Anterior choroidal artery</u> (see below)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Contralateral</u> <u>hemiplegia</u> (lower limbs affected more severely)<br><br>* Minimal hemisensory loss (lower limbs affected more severely)<br><br>* <u>Dysarthria</u><br><br>* <u>Aphasia</u><br><br>* <u>Abulia</u> (absence of motivation)<br><br>* Limb <u>apraxia</u><br><br>* <u>Urinary incontinence</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Middle cerebral artery (<u>MCA</u>)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> cortex, including:<br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> portion of the frontal and <u>parietal lobes</u>: motor and sensory cortex of the face and upper extremities<br><br>* <u>Temporal lobe</u>: <u>Wernicke area</u><br><br>* <u>Frontal lobe</u>: <u>Broca area</u><br><br>* <u>Lenticulostriate arteries</u> supply deeper structures of the <u>brain</u>:<br><br>* <u>Putamen</u>, <u>globus pallidus</u><br><br>* Parts of the <u>internal capsule</u> and <u>caudate nucleus</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Lenticulostriate arteries<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Contralateral</u> <u>hemiplegia</u><br><br>* <u>Contralateral</u> hemisensory loss<br><br>* Gaze deviation towards the side of <u>infarction</u><br><br>* <u>Hemineglect</u> (right <u>MCA</u> territory, nondominant hemisphere)<br><br>* <u>Contralateral</u> <u>homonymous hemianopia</u> without <u>macular sparing</u><br><br>* <u>Broca aphasia</u> (inferior frontal <u>gyrus</u> of dominant hemisphere)<br><br>* <u>Wernicke aphasia</u> (<u>superior temporal gyrus</u> of dominant hemisphere)<br><br><br> |
| <br>Anterior choroidal artery [[2]](/library/u4YpO6) | <br><br>* <u>Optic tract</u> and <u>lateral geniculate nuclei</u><br><br>* <u>Hippocampus</u> and <u>lateral</u> <u>thalamus</u><br><br>* <u>Posterior</u> limb of the <u>internal capsule</u><br><br><br> | <br>* N/A<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Hemiparesis</u> or <u>hemiplegia</u> (including <u>dysarthria</u>)<br><br>* Hemisensory loss<br><br>* <u>Homonymous hemianopsia</u> (with sparing of the horizontal median <u>visual field</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Posterior</u> circulation (branch of the <u>basilar artery</u>) |  |  |  |
| <br>Posterior cerebral artery (PCA) | <br>* Posteroinferior cortex<br><br>* Occipital lobes<br><br>* Posteromedial aspect of the <u>temporal lobes</u><br><br>* <u>Thalamus</u><br><br> | <br>* Several branches to the cortical lobes and <u>choroid plexus</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Contralateral</u> hemisensory loss<br><br>* <u>Contralateral</u> <u>homonymous hemianopia</u> with <u>macular sparing</u><br><br>* <u>Memory</u> deficits<br><br>* <u>Vertigo</u>, <u>nausea</u><br><br>* Left PCA: <u>alexia without agraphia</u>, <u>anomic aphasia</u>, <u>visual agnosia</u><br><br>* Right PCA: <u>prosopagnosia</u><br><br><br> |

## Venous drainage

The cerebral hemispheres are drained by <u>superficial</u> and deep cerebral <u>veins</u>, which drain into the <u>dural venous sinuses</u>.




### <u>Superficial</u> cerebral <u>veins</u>




| Overview of <u>superficial</u> cerebral <u>veins</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <br><u>Superficial veins</u><br>Drain the <u>white matter</u><br> | <br>Bridging vein <br> | Draining venous sinus |
| Superior cerebral <u>veins</u> | Superior anastomotic <u>vein</u><br> | <u>Superior sagittal sinus</u> |
| Middle cerebral <u>veins</u> | Inferior anastomotic <u>vein</u><br> | <u>Cavernous sinus</u> |
| Inferior cerebral <u>veins</u> | N/A | Cavernous and <u>transverse venous sinuses</u><br> |





### Deep cerebral <u>veins</u>




Deep cerebral <u>veins</u> drain the cerebral medulla and drain into the straight sinus.




* Medullary <u>veins</u>: drain the <u>gray matter</u>

* Subependymal <u>veins</u>: receive blood from the medullary <u>veins</u>

* Basal vein (<u>vein of Rosenthal</u>): paired paramedian <u>veins</u> that receive blood from the <u>temporal lobe</u> and drain into the <u>great cerebral vein</u>

* Great cerebral vein (<u>vein of Galen</u>): receives blood from the <u>deep veins</u>





### <u>Dural venous sinuses</u>




* The dural venous sinuses drain blood from cerebral <u>veins</u> and <u>CSF</u> from the <u>arachnoid granulations</u> into the <u>internal jugular vein</u>.

* The sinuses are located intracranially between the two layers of <u>dura mater</u> (endosteal layer and <u>meningeal layer</u>).





| Venous sinus |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Location | Characteristics |
| Superior sagittal sinus | <br>* At the midline<br><br> | <br><br>* Terminates at the <u>confluence of sinuses</u><br><br>* Becomes the right <u>transverse sinus</u><br><br>* Drains blood from cortical <u>veins</u> of the cerebral hemispheres<br><br>* Main location of cerebral fluid return via <u>arachnoid granulations</u><br><br><br> |
| Inferior sagittal sinus | <br>* At the midline<br><br> | <br><br>* Joined by the <u>great cerebral vein of Galen</u> before draining into the straight sinus<br><br>* Drains blood from the <u>medial</u> surface of the cerebral hemispheres<br><br><br> |
| Straight sinus | <br>* At the midline<br><br> | <br><br>* Terminates at the <u>confluence of sinuses</u><br><br>* May unite with the left <u>transverse sinus</u> (variant)<br><br><br> |
| Occipital sinus | <br>* Posteriorly<br><br> | <br>* Drains into the <u>confluence of sinuses</u><br><br> |
| Confluence of sinuses | <br>* Posteriorly<br><br> | <br><br>* Formed by the union of the <u>superior sagittal sinus</u>, straight sinus, and occipital sinus<br><br>* Drains into left and right <u>transverse sinus</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Superior petrosal sinus (paired) | <br>* Laterally<br><br> | <br><br>* Drains into the <u>transverse sinus</u><br><br>* Drains blood from the <u>inner ear</u> structures via the labyrinthine <u>vein</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Transverse sinus (paired) | <br>* Laterally along the edge of the <u>tentorium cerebelli</u><br><br> | <br>* Drains into the sigmoid sinus<br><br> |
| <br>Inferior petrosal sinus (paired) | <br>* Laterally<br><br> | <br><br>* Drains the <u>cavernous sinus</u> into the <u>internal jugular vein</u><br><br>* Drains blood from the medulla, <u>pons</u>, and inferior surface of the <u>cerebellum</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Sigmoid sinus (paired) | <br>* Laterally<br><br> | <br>* Continuation of <u>transverse sinus</u> that arches downward in an S-shaped groove into the <u>internal jugular vein</u><br><br> |
| <br>Sphenoparietal sinus (paired) | <br>* Anteriorly<br><br> | <br>* Drains into the <u>cavernous sinus</u><br><br> |
| <br>Cavernous sinus (paired) | <br>* Anteriorly on each side of the <u>sella turcica</u> (<u>pituitary</u> fossa)<br><br> | <br><br>* Structures running through these sinuses include:<br><br>* Medially: <u>internal carotid artery</u> with <u>postganglionic</u> <u>sympathetic</u> fibers and <u>abducens nerve</u> (<u>CN VI</u>)<br><br>* Laterally: <u>oculomotor nerve</u> (<u>CN III</u>), <u>trochlear nerve</u> (<u>CN IV</u>), <u>ophthalmic nerve</u> (<u>CN V<sub>1</sub></u>), and <u>maxillary nerve</u> (<u>CN V<sub>2</sub></u>)<br><br>* Receives the superior <u>ophthalmic vein</u> (blood from <u>eye</u> and <u>superficial</u> cortex)<br><br>* Drains into the petrosal sinuses and then into <u>internal jugular vein</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Basilar venous plexus (paired) | <br>* Over the basilar part of the <u>occipital bone</u> (the clivus)<br><br> | <br>* Connected with the cavernous and petrosal sinuses and the internal <u>vertebral</u> (epidural) venous plexus. [[3]](/library/w4Yhl6)<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> Cerebral <u>veins</u> run in the <u>subarachnoid space</u>, have no valves to allow bidirectional blood flow, and have no muscular layer in the vessel wall.

## Cerebral blood flow regulation

* Neurometabolic coupling: enables adequate delivery of <u>nutrients</u> or substrates to areas with increased neural activity

* Neurovascular coupling (functional <u>hyperemia</u>): enables adequate delivery of oxygen through constriction or dilation of <u>microvessels</u> to areas with increased neural activity





> [!TIP]
> Therapeutic <u>hyperventilation</u> reduces <u>pCO<sub>2</sub></u> → ↓ cerebral blood flow → ↓ intracranial pressure (e.g., used when patients with acute <u>cerebral edema</u> are unresponsive to other treatments).

---

## Clinical significance

* Arterial conditions

* <u>Stroke</u>

* <u>Cerebral aneurysms</u>

* <u>Subarachnoid hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Epidural hematoma</u>

* <u>Intraparenchymal hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Trigeminal neuralgia</u> (compression of <u>superior cerebellar artery</u>)

* Hydrostatic <u>cerebral edema</u> (e.g., in severe <u>hypertension</u>)

* Venous conditions

* <u>Cerebral venous thrombosis</u>

* <u>Cavernous sinus syndrome</u>

* <u>Subdural hematoma</u> (caused by ruptured <u>bridging veins</u>)
